modules.title: Work out powers

chapter.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2⁵ means 2 multiplied by itself 5 times. The small raised number (the power) counts how many 2s there are; it is not a number to multiply by.

chapter.title: Laws of exponents with one base
text: A power counts how many times the base is multiplied. Multiplying joins the factors (add the powers), dividing cancels them (subtract), and a power of a power repeats them (multiply).
aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ, aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ, (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ. A negative power means a fraction: a⁻² = 1/a².
math: Write 9¹⁰ × 9³ as a single power of 9, that is 9 to the power □. What number goes in the box?

chapter.title: The units digit of a large power
text: Only the units digit affects the units digit of a product, and the units digits of powers repeat in a short cycle.
Write the units digits of the first few powers until they repeat. Divide the power by the cycle length; the remainder tells the place in the cycle (remainder 0 means the last place).
math: What is the units digit of 19⁵⁸?
Units digits of the powers of 9 repeat: 9, 1, …
58 ÷ 2 leaves the place 2 in the cycle

chapter.title: Zero and negative powers
text: Each step down in the power divides by the base once: 2³ = 8, 2² = 4, 2¹ = 2, 2⁰ = 1, 2⁻¹ = 1/2, 2⁻² = 1/4.
Combine the powers first (add them, keeping the signs), then a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ.

screens.title: Count them out
text: Write the number as many times as the power says, with × between them. Then multiply two at a time.

strategies.title: Build it up one step at a time

screens.title: Multiply again and again
text: Start with the number and multiply by it again for each extra power: for 3⁴, 3 → 9 → 27 → 81. That is one multiplication fewer than the power.

strategies.title: Use the multiplication facts you know

screens.title: Each step is a fact
text: Every step of a power is a multiplication fact: 2 × 2 = 4, 4 × 2 = 8, 8 × 2 = 16. If a step is slow, say that times table first.

modules.title: Differentiate powers of x

chapter.title: The power rule
text: To differentiate k xⁿ, bring the power down as a factor and lower the power by one: the derivative is k n xⁿ⁻¹. Then put in the value of x.
chapter.tip: Lower the power first, then substitute.

chapter.title: Differentiating k xⁿ times sin(ax) or cos(ax)
text: When y = u × v, a small change in x changes both factors: y′ = u′v + uv′. The derivative of sin(ax) is a cos(ax), and of cos(ax) is −a sin(ax).
Name u and v, differentiate each (remember the inner factor a), then write u′v + uv′.
math: Differentiate y = 5x^3 sin(x) with respect to x.

strategies.title: A derivative is a rate of change

screens.title: Not the value: how fast it changes
text: f′(3) is how fast f is changing at x = 3, not the value f(3). For f(x) = x², the values at 2.9, 3 and 3.1 are 8.41, 9 and 9.61: they rise by 1.2 over 0.2, which is 6 per unit, and the rule gives 2 × 3 = 6.

screens.title: In this order
text: Multiply the coefficient by the power, then take one off the power. Only then put in the number.

screens.title: A power is repeated multiplication
text: 2² = 2 × 2 = 4 and 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. A power is not the number times the power: 2³ is not 6.

modules.title: Integrate powers of x

chapter.title: Reverse the power rule
text: Differentiating xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) gives xⁿ. So an antiderivative of k xⁿ is k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1): raise the power by one, then divide by the new power.
math: ∫ k xⁿ dx = k xⁿ⁺¹ ⁄ (n + 1) + C

chapter.title: Between two limits
text: For a definite integral, work out the antiderivative F at the upper limit and at the lower limit, then subtract: F(upper) − F(lower). The constant C cancels.
math: Raise the power and divide: F(x) = 3x³ ⁄ 3

screens.title: Undo, then check
text: Whatever antiderivative you write, differentiate it: you must get back the function you started with. x³ differentiates to 3x², so ∫ 3x² dx = x³ + C.

screens.title: Two moves, then the limits
text: Add one to the power, then divide by that new power. Then put in the upper limit and the lower limit, and subtract.
math: Raise the power and divide: F(x) = 12x² ⁄ 2

screens.title: What the working needs
text: The working needs powers (2³ = 8) and fractions with the same denominator (16⁄3 − 2⁄3 = 14⁄3). If either is slow, practise it first; the integration itself is two moves.

modules.title: Integrate by substitution

chapter.title: Spot u and du
text: In ∫ 2x(x² + 1)² dx, call the inside of the bracket u = x² + 1. Its derivative, 2x, is already there: du = 2x dx. So the integral is ∫ u² du.

chapter.title: Change the limits
text: With limits, change them too: put each x limit into u = x² + 1, and integrate between those u values. You never go back to x.
chapter.tip: Using the x limits for u is the most common slip.
math: Let u = x² + 1: x = 0 gives u = 1, x = 1 gives u = 2
2x dx = du, so the integral is ∫ u² du = u³ ⁄ 3

screens.title: Nothing left to divide by
text: du ⁄ dx = 2x, so a small change dx in x changes u by 2x dx. The 2x in the integral is exactly what turns dx into du: there is no extra 2 to divide by.

strategies.title: Make a little table of limits

screens.title: x row, u row
text: Write two rows, x and u. Under x put the two limits; under u put x² + c for each. Then integrate in u between the u values.
math: Let u = x² + 2: x = 0 gives u = 2, x = 1 gives u = 3
2x dx = du, so the integral is ∫ u¹ du = u² ⁄ 2

screens.title: The last step is arithmetic
text: The last step is powers of whole numbers, like 2³ = 8 and 5³ = 125, then a subtraction and a division. A power is repeated multiplication, not the number times the power.

modules.title: How many solutions? The discriminant

chapter.title: b² − 4ac decides
text: For ax² + bx + c = 0, work out the discriminant b² − 4ac. Positive: two different real solutions. Zero: one (repeated) solution. Negative: no real solutions.
chapter.tip: b² is never negative, even when b is.
math: How many different real solutions does x² + 2x + 5 = 0 have?

screens.title: Crossings
text: y = x² + bx + c is a U-shaped curve. Two solutions: it crosses the x-axis twice. One: it just touches it. None: it stays above it. The discriminant tells you which, without drawing.

strategies.title: Write each part with its sign

screens.title: b², then 4ac, then subtract
text: Write b², then 4ac with c's own sign, then subtract. For x² − 4x − 5: b² = 16, 4ac = 4 × (−5) = −20, and 16 − (−20) = 36, which is positive: two solutions.
math: How many different real solutions does x² − x + 3 = 0 have?

screens.title: Two sign facts
text: Taking away a negative number adds: 16 − (−20) = 36. And a square is never negative: (−4)² = 16.

4 hundred and 5 = 405; put the periods together

modules.title: Finding a missing digit in a sum or difference

chapter.title: Finding a missing digit in a sum or difference
text: A sum or difference is a true sentence, so each column must work out, including any regrouping with the column on its right (a ten carried in, or 1 exchanged for 10 ones).
math: Find the missing digit: 390 − 232 = 1□8. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right is regrouped: 1 from this column is exchanged for 10 there, so this column has 1 less
Work the hidden column, using the exchange: the missing digit is 5
chapter.tip: In that column the smaller digit was taken from the larger one. When the top digit is smaller, regroup first: exchange 1 from the next column on the left for 10 in this column.

chapter.title: Winning move in a take-away game
text: Work backwards from the end. Some numbers of counters are "safe" to leave for the other player: from them, whatever they take, you can get back to the next safe number.
If each turn takes 1 to k, the safe numbers go up in steps of k + 1 (0, k + 1, 2(k + 1) … when the last counter wins; 1 more than these when it loses). Take enough to leave a safe number.
math: There are 26 counters in the picture. Two players take turns. On each turn a player removes 1, 2 or 3 counters. The player who takes the last counter wins. It is your turn. How many counters should you take now so that you can always win?
Whatever the other player takes, you can make the pair of turns add up to 4. So leave a number that is a multiple of 4

screens.title: The method
text: Start from the ones column and move left. In each column, note whether the column regroups: a ten carried (addition) or 1 exchanged for 10 in the column on the right (subtraction), then find the digit that makes the hidden column right. Check by doing the whole calculation.
math: Find the missing digit: 387 − 169 = □18. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right needs no regrouping (nothing is carried or exchanged)
Work the hidden column, using the exchange: the missing digit is 2

screens.title: Try the digits and check
text: Put a digit in the box and work out the whole sum.
If it is not right, see whether the answer came out too big or too small and try a better digit. Only one digit works.
math: Find the missing digit: 5□4 + 281 = 835. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right needs no regrouping (nothing is carried or exchanged)
Work the hidden column, using the carry: the missing digit is 5

screens.title: Undo the operation
text: A missing part of an addition is total − other part.
A missing first number of a subtraction is answer + number taken away. Work out that calculation and read off the digit.
math: Find the missing digit: 8□1 − 363 = 508. Which digit goes in the box □?
The column to the right is regrouped: 1 from this column is exchanged for 10 there, so this column has 1 less
Work the hidden column, using the exchange: the missing digit is 7

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the missing digit: 427 + 405 = 8□2. Which digit goes in the box □?” A common wrong answer is 2.
The ten carried from the column on the right was forgotten. When a column adds up to 10 or more, 1 goes to the next column.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Subtract with regrouping. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.

modules.title: Counting every combination (one from each group)

chapter.title: Counting every combination (one from each group)
text: Every choice from one group can be matched with every choice from the next, so the number of combinations is the product of the numbers of choices.
math: The table shows Imran's 2 shirts and 3 pairs of shorts. An outfit is one shirt with one pair of shorts. How many different outfits are possible?
Each of the 2 first choices goes with each of the 3 second choices: 2 × 3 = 6
chapter.tip: The numbers of choices were added. Each choice from the first group goes with every choice from the next, so multiply.

chapter.title: How many numbers can be made from given digits
text: Fill the places one at a time from the left. The number of ways is the product of the choices for each place.
Count the choices for the first place (0 is not allowed there), then for the next place (one fewer if digits cannot repeat), and so on; multiply.
math: How many different 2-digit numbers can you make from the digits 3, 5, 7, 0, if a digit may be used more than once?
Choices for each place, from the left: 3 × 4

screens.title: The method
text: Fix the first choice and count how many ways the rest can go; that number is the same for every first choice, so multiply. With a third group, multiply again.
math: The table shows a canteen's 6 main dishes, 2 side dishes and 3 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?
Each of the 6 first choices goes with each of the 2 second choices: 6 × 2 = 12
Each of those 12 goes with each of the 3 last choices: 12 × 3 = 36

screens.title: Make an organised list
text: Take the first shirt and list it with every skirt, then the second shirt with every skirt, and so on.
Each row of the list has the same length, so the total is rows × length of a row.
math: The table shows a canteen's 6 main dishes, 2 side dishes and 4 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?
Each of the 6 first choices goes with each of the 2 second choices: 6 × 2 = 12
Each of those 12 goes with each of the 4 last choices: 12 × 4 = 48

screens.title: Draw a tree
text: Draw one branch for each first choice; from the end of each, draw one branch for each second choice.
Count the ends of the last branches.
math: The table shows a canteen's 3 main dishes, 3 side dishes and 2 sweets. A meal is one main dish, one side dish and one sweet. How many different meals are possible?
Each of the 3 first choices goes with each of the 3 second choices: 3 × 3 = 9
Each of those 9 goes with each of the 2 last choices: 9 × 2 = 18

chapter.title: Reading a pie chart
text: A pie chart shows the whole group as a full circle; each part's size is a fraction of the whole group.

chapter.title: Sector angles in a pie chart
text: The whole group is the whole circle, 360°. Each part gets the same fraction of 360° as it is of the group.

chapter.title: Writing a number rule with a letter
text: A letter stands for any number. A rule written with the letter works for every number at once.

chapter.title: Continuing square, triangular and other number patterns
text: Square numbers come from square dot pictures (n rows of n), triangular numbers from triangles (1 + 2 + … + n), rectangular numbers from n rows of n + 1.

text: A claim that says 'every' must work for ALL numbers. One number where it fails, a counterexample, is enough to show it is not always true; numbers where it works never prove it.
math: Selvi says: "Every number that ends in 6 is a multiple of 4." Selvi tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?
Test each number: 106 fits the first part of the claim but not the second, so it is a counterexample
chapter.tip: 16 agrees with the claim, so it does not show the claim is wrong. To show a claim is not always true, find ONE number where it fails.

screens.title: The method
text: Test each number: does it fit the first part of the claim? If yes, does the rest of the claim hold? The number that fits the first part but not the rest is the counterexample.
math: Farhan says: "Every multiple of 3 is an odd number." Farhan tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?
Test each number: 48 fits the first part of the claim but not the second, so it is a counterexample

screens.title: Two ticks
text: Make two columns: 'is it one the claim talks about?' and 'does the claim hold?'.
The counterexample has a tick in the first column and a cross in the second.
math: Farhan says: "Every multiple of 3 is an odd number." Farhan tests the numbers in the table. Which one of them shows that the claim is NOT always true?
Test each number: 90 fits the first part of the claim but not the second, so it is a counterexample

chapter.title: Solving a one-step equation
text: An equation is a balance: both sides have the same value. Doing the opposite operation to both sides keeps it balanced and leaves x alone.

modules.title: Collecting like terms

chapter.title: Collecting like terms
text: Like terms have the same letter part: 3x and −5x are like terms, 3x and 2y are not. Like terms can be added because they count the same thing.
chapter.tip: x terms and y terms were added together into one term. Only like terms (the same letter) can be added: x terms with x terms, y terms with y terms.

chapter.title: Subtracting one expression from another
text: Taking away a bracket takes away every term inside it, so each sign in the bracket changes: −(3x − 4) = −3x + 4.
Remove the brackets, changing every sign in the second one. Then collect the x terms and the number terms.
math: −(10x + 12) = −10x − 12: every sign in the bracket changes

chapter.title: Coefficients and the constant term
text: An expression is a sum of terms. Each term is a number (the coefficient, with its sign) times letters; a term with no letter is the constant term.
Split the expression at each + or −, keeping the sign with the term after it. The coefficient is the signed number in front of the letters; no number means 1.
math: In the expression 7x² − 8xy − 4y − 4, what is the constant term?
The constant term is the term with no letter: −4

chapter.title: The top of a number pyramid
text: In a four-row pyramid the corner blocks of the bottom row reach the top once and the two middle blocks reach it 3 times each, so the top is 1, 3, 3, 1 times the bottom blocks.

Keep adding pairs to the top and collect like terms: x + 49

screens.title: The method
text: Group the x terms and the y terms, keeping each sign with the term after it. Add the numbers in front of each group and write one term for each letter.

modules.title: An expression for a growing pattern

chapter.title: An expression for a growing pattern
text: If a pattern grows by the same amount d each time, Figure n is d × n plus a fixed part. The fixed part is what makes Figure 1 come out right.
math: A pattern of figures uses 11, 14, 17 and 20 square tiles for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of square tiles. Write an expression for the number of square tiles in Figure n.
Each figure adds 14 − 11 = 3, so the expression has 3n
chapter.tip: The rule 'add 3 each time' was written as n + 3. Figure n has 3 added n times, which is 3n, plus a fixed part.

chapter.title: Why a 'think of a number' trick works
text: Using a letter for the number lets you follow the trick for every number at once. When the added numbers cancel, the answer depends only on n, which is why the trick always works.
Write each step as an expression, using brackets when a whole result is multiplied. Expand the brackets and collect like terms.
math: Think of a number n. Multiply it by 3. Add 3. Multiply the result by 5. Then take away 15. Write a simplified expression for the final result.
The numbers cancel, leaving 15n: the result is always 15 times the starting number

screens.title: The method
text: Find how many are added each time: that number multiplies n. Then compare d × 1 with Figure 1 to find what to add or take away. Check with Figure 2.
math: A pattern of figures uses 12, 17, 22 and 27 matchsticks for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of matchsticks. Write an expression for the number of matchsticks in Figure n.
Each figure adds 17 − 12 = 5, so the expression has 5n

screens.title: Go back to Figure 0
text: Step back once from Figure 1: Figure 0 would have (Figure 1) − d.
That is the fixed part; then add d for each figure: d n + (Figure 0).
math: A pattern of figures uses 8, 12, 16 and 20 square tiles for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of square tiles. Write an expression for the number of square tiles in Figure n.
Each figure adds 12 − 8 = 4, so the expression has 4n

strategies.title: See the groups in the picture

screens.title: See the groups in the picture
text: In a row of squares made of matchsticks, each new square needs 3 more sticks and the first square needs one extra.
So n squares need 3n + 1 sticks: 3 for each square, plus the first stick.
math: A pattern of figures uses 13, 21, 29 and 37 matchsticks for Figures 1, 2, 3 and 4. Each figure adds the same number of matchsticks. Write an expression for the number of matchsticks in Figure n.
Each figure adds 21 − 13 = 8, so the expression has 8n

modules.title: Terms from a recursive rule

chapter.title: Terms from a recursive rule
text: A recursive rule tells you how to get each term from the one before it; the first term starts the chain.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 2 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ + 2. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).
chapter.tip: 2 was added before multiplying by 2. The rule multiplies the term first, then adds.

chapter.title: From a recursive rule to a formula for tₙ
text: Adding d each time means tₙ is the first term plus (n − 1) steps of d: tₙ = t₁ + (n − 1)d.
Write t₁ + (n − 1)d with the numbers, open the bracket and collect the numbers. Check that n = 1 gives t₁ and n = 2 gives t₂.
math: A sequence has t₁ = −9 and tₙ₊₁ = tₙ + 3. Write a formula for tₙ in terms of n.
From t₁ to tₙ there are n − 1 steps of 3: 3n − 3

chapter.title: A Virahanka-Fibonacci style sequence
text: Each new term is made from the two terms before it, so you must keep the last two terms in view as you go.
Write the terms in a numbered row: add the last two to get the next, until you reach the term you need.
math: A sequence begins 8, 9, and every term after that is the sum of the two terms just before it. What is term number 5?

screens.title: The method
text: Write t₁. Put it into the rule to get t₂, put t₂ in to get t₃, and so on. Do the operations in the order the rule gives.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 2 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ + 3. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).

strategies.title: A table of n and tₙ

screens.title: A table of n and tₙ
text: Make two columns: n = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and tₙ.
Fill each row from the row above using the rule, showing the working.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 8 and tₙ₊₁ = tₙ + 1. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).

screens.title: A number machine
text: Think of the rule as a machine: a term goes in, the next term comes out.
Feed each output back in as the next input.
math: A sequence has t₁ = 5 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ + 3. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A sequence has t₁ = 9 and tₙ₊₁ = 2tₙ − 3. Write the first five terms as (t₁, t₂, t₃, t₄, t₅).” A common wrong answer is (9, 12, 18, 30, 54).
3 was taken away before multiplying by 2. The rule multiplies the term first, then takes away.
A recursive rule tells you how to get each term from the one before it; the first term starts the chain.

modules.title: An inverse proportion

chapter.title: An inverse proportion
text: In an inverse proportion, when one quantity is multiplied by some number the other is divided by it, so their product never changes (workers × days = the total work).
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 4, y = 3. What is y when x = 3?
chapter.tip: The product 4 × 3 = 12 is right, but it must then be shared by 3.

chapter.title: Time taken working together
text: Think of the work done in one day: a person who takes p days does 1/p of the job each day. Working together, the parts done per day add up.
Add 1/p and 1/q to get the part of the job done in one day together; the number of days is 1 divided by that fraction.
math: Arjun can finish a job alone in 3 days, and Meena can finish it alone in 9 days. Working together at the same rates, how many days will they take?
Part of the job done in one day together: 1/3 + 1/9 = 4/9

screens.title: The method
text: Multiply the two given values to get the fixed product, then divide it by the new value.
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 3, y = 24. What is y when x = 12?

screens.title: Go through one worker
text: If a workers take d days, 1 worker takes a × d days (one person does all the work).
Then b workers share it: (a × d) ÷ b days.
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 3, y = 16. What is y when x = 2?

screens.title: Invert the ratio
text: If x becomes twice as big, y becomes half as big.
So y(new) = y(old) × x(old) ÷ x(new).
math: x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 4, y = 3. What is y when x = 6?

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “x and y are in inverse proportion. When x = 8, y = 10. What is y when x = 10?” A common wrong answer is 80.
The product 8 × 10 = 80 is right, but it must then be shared by 10.
In an inverse proportion, when one quantity is multiplied by some number the other is divided by it, so their product never changes (workers × days = the total work).

modules.title: The third angle of a triangle

chapter.title: The third angle of a triangle
text: The three angles of any triangle add up to 180°: tear off the corners and they fit together on a straight line.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 35° and 90°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?
chapter.tip: The angles were taken from 360°. The three angles of a triangle add up to 180°; 360° is the sum around a point or in a quadrilateral.

chapter.title: The exterior angle of a triangle
text: An exterior angle and the interior angle next to it make a straight line (180°), and the three interior angles also make 180°, so the exterior angle equals the two far interior angles together.
To find the exterior angle, add the two interior opposite angles. To find one of those, subtract the other from the exterior angle.
math: One side of a triangle is extended. The two interior angles opposite the exterior angle are 31° and 118°. What is the exterior angle, in degrees?
Exterior angle = sum of the interior opposite angles: 31° + 118° = 149°

chapter.title: Angles of an isosceles triangle
text: In an isosceles triangle the angles opposite the two equal sides are equal; with the angle sum of 180°, one angle tells you the other two.
Vertex angle known: take it from 180° and halve. Base angle known: double it and take that from 180°.
math: In an isosceles triangle each of the two equal angles (opposite the equal sides) is 62°. What is the third angle, in degrees?

chapter.title: How long can the third side be?
text: In a triangle, any two sides together are longer than the third. So the third side is less than the sum of the other two and more than their difference.
Longest: one less than the sum of the two sides. Shortest: one more than their difference (for whole numbers).
math: Two sides of a triangle are 4 cm and 14 cm. The third side is a whole number of centimetres. What is the longest it can be, in cm?
The third side must be less than 4 + 14 = 18 cm
The longest whole number below 18 is 17

screens.title: The method
text: Add the two angles you know, then take the sum from 180°.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 56° and 85°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?

screens.title: Tear off the corners
text: Cut out a paper triangle, tear off its three corners and place them side by side.
They make a straight line, which is 180°.

screens.title: Count on to 180
text: Start from the sum of the two angles and count up to 180 in easy jumps (to the next ten, then tens).
The total of the jumps is the third angle.
math: Two angles of a triangle are 85° and 49°, as in the picture (not to scale). What is the third angle, in degrees?

modules.title: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles

chapter.title: Corresponding parts of congruent triangles
text: When ΔABC ≅ ΔXYZ, the letters are written in matching order: A goes with X, B with Y, C with Z. Matching parts are equal.
math: In triangle ABC, AB = 7 cm, BC = 9 cm and CA = 4 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle QRP. What is the length of RP, in cm?
In the statement, RP sits in the same places as BC, so RP = BC = 9 cm
chapter.tip: P, Q, R were matched with A, B, C in alphabetical order. The order of the letters in the congruence statement shows the matching: the first letters match, the second letters match, and the third letters match.

screens.title: The method
text: Write the two names one above the other. Find the asked letters in the second name, read the letters above them in the first name, and use that side or angle.
math: In triangle ABC, AB = 9 cm, BC = 10 cm and CA = 8 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle RQP. What is the length of QR, in cm?
In the statement, QR sits in the same places as BA, so QR = BA = 9 cm

screens.title: Stack the names
text: Write A B C on one line and the second triangle's name under it.
Each column is a matching pair of vertices; a side is two columns.
math: In triangle ABC, AB = 4 cm, BC = 7 cm and CA = 6 cm. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle RQP. What is the length of PQ, in cm?
In the statement, PQ sits in the same places as CB, so PQ = CB = 7 cm

screens.title: Trace and place
text: Imagine tracing triangle ABC and placing the tracing exactly on the other triangle.
Each vertex lands on its matching vertex, so matching sides lie on top of each other.
math: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 50°, ∠B = 75° and ∠C = 55°. Triangle ABC ≅ triangle QPR. What is ∠P, in degrees?
In the statement, P sits in the same places as B, so P = B = 75°

text: In a right-angled triangle the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides (Baudhayana's rule for the diagonal of a rectangle).

chapter.title: The missing angle at a point of a tiling
text: Tiles fit around a point with no gaps or overlaps only when their corner angles add up to exactly 360°.
math: At one point of a floor tiling, one regular pentagon and one regular nonagon meet, together with one more tile, with no gaps and no overlaps. What angle must the corner of the last tile be, in degrees?

Each corner of a regular 9-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 9 = 140°

Each corner of a regular 12-sided polygon is 180° − 360° ÷ 12 = 150°

chapter.title: Slant height and surface area of a cone
text: Cut a cone's curved surface along a slant line and flatten it: it becomes a sector of a circle of radius l whose arc is the base circumference 2πr, so its area is ½ × 2πr × l = πrl.

chapter.title: Volume of a cone

text: A sphere's surface is exactly four circles of the same radius (4πr²), and its volume is 4/3 πr³. A hemisphere is half a sphere: curved surface 2πr², volume 2/3 πr³.

modules.title: Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction

chapter.title: Writing a recurring decimal as a fraction
text: A recurring decimal is rational: multiplying by a power of 10 shifts the repeating part, and subtracting makes the endless tail cancel.
math: Write 2.454545… (the block 45 repeats for ever) as a fraction p/q.
Multiply by 100 and subtract: 100x − x removes the repeating block: 99x = 243
chapter.tip: The decimal was cut off after two digits. A repeating block of two digits goes over 99, not 100.

chapter.title: Will the decimal terminate or recur?
text: A fraction in its simplest form terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5, because only then can it be written over a power of 10.
Simplify the fraction first. Factorise the denominator: only 2s and 5s means it terminates; any other prime means it recurs.
math: Without dividing it out, decide what kind of decimal expansion 40/100 has.
Look at the denominator's prime factors: denominator 5: only 2s and 5s

chapter.title: How many decimal places before a fraction terminates
text: p/(2^m 5^n) can be rewritten over 10^k, where k is the larger of m and n, so it has exactly k decimal places (after simplifying).
Simplify the fraction, write the denominator as 2^m × 5^n, and take the larger power.
math: 11/8000 has a terminating decimal expansion. After how many decimal places does it terminate?

chapter.title: Picking out the irrational number
text: A number is rational if it can be written as p/q with whole numbers p and q (q ≠ 0); its decimal stops or repeats. √n is irrational unless n is a perfect square.
Simplify each number first: √49 = 7, √2 × √8 = √16 = 4, (√5)² = 5, a repeating decimal is a fraction. Whatever is still a non-square root is irrational.
math: Which one of these numbers is irrational?
Irrational: √19/3 cannot be written as p/q, because 19 is not a perfect square

screens.title: The method
text: Let x be the number. Multiply by 10 for one repeating digit, by 100 for two, and subtract so the repeating tails cancel; then divide and simplify.
math: Write 2.474747… (the block 47 repeats for ever) as a fraction p/q.
Multiply by 100 and subtract: 100x − x removes the repeating block: 99x = 245

screens.title: The nines rule
text: 0.ddd… = d/9 and 0.ababab… = ab/99.
If one digit comes before the repeat, as in 0.2777…, use (27 − 2)/90.
math: Write 2.393939… (the block 39 repeats for ever) as a fraction p/q.
Multiply by 100 and subtract: 100x − x removes the repeating block: 99x = 237

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Write 2.464646… (the block 46 repeats for ever) as a fraction p/q.” A common wrong answer is 2.46.
The decimal was cut off after two digits. A repeating block of two digits goes over 99, not 100.

modules.title: The least non-negative residue modulo n

chapter.title: The least non-negative residue modulo n
text: a ≡ r (mod n) means n divides a − r. Every integer is congruent to exactly one of 0, 1, …, n − 1 — its least non-negative residue.
math: Find the least non-negative integer r such that 174 ≡ r (mod 7).
The largest multiple of 7 not above 174 is 7 × 24 = 168
174 − (168) = 6, which is between 0 and the modulus
chapter.tip: The quotient (24) was given; the congruence asks for the remainder.

chapter.title: Solving a linear congruence ax ≡ b (mod n)
text: ax ≡ b (mod n) asks for x so that a × x leaves remainder b. Since b, b + n, b + 2n … are all ≡ b, one of them divides exactly by a.
Write b, b + n, b + 2n, … until one is a multiple of a; divide it by a. Check: a times your answer leaves remainder b.
math: Solve 5x ≡ 5 (mod 11). Give the least non-negative solution x.
Add 11 to 5 (0 times) until it divides by the coefficient: 5

chapter.title: Day of the week after d days (modulo 7)
text: The days repeat every 7, so d days from today land on the same day as d mod 7 days from today.
Divide d by 7 and keep the remainder. Count that many days forward from today (tomorrow is 1).
math: Today is Thursday. Which day of the week will it be 152 days from today?
Count 5 days on from Thursday: Tuesday

screens.title: The method
text: Find the largest multiple of n that is not more than the number (for a negative number this multiple is more negative), then subtract it.
math: Find the least non-negative integer r such that 213 ≡ r (mod 4).
The largest multiple of 4 not above 213 is 4 × 53 = 212
213 − (212) = 1, which is between 0 and the modulus

screens.title: Wrap around a clock
text: Think of a clock with n hours marked 0 to n − 1.
Moving a steps from 0 lands on the residue: every full turn of n steps brings you back to 0, and going backwards is turning the other way.
math: Find the least non-negative integer r such that 73 ≡ r (mod 9).
The largest multiple of 9 not above 73 is 9 × 8 = 72
73 − (72) = 1, which is between 0 and the modulus

chapter.title: Deciding the shape of three points from their distances
text: Distances decide the shape: if the two shorter distances add up to the longest, the points are on one line; if their squares add up to the square of the longest, there is a right angle (Pythagoras' converse); two equal distances make an isosceles triangle.

chapter.title: The largest product from four digits

The two largest digits, 9 and 4, go in the tens places (each counts ten times)

math: Can 119ⁿ end with the digit 0 for some natural number n? Choose the statement that is true.
119: 2 does not divide it; 5 does not divide it
Ending in 0 means divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, and the primes in aⁿ are exactly the primes in a: neither

chapter.title: The domain of a real function
text: The domain of a real function is every real x for which the formula gives a real number: what is under a square root must be ≥ 0, and a denominator must not be 0.

chapter.title: The range of a quadratic function
text: Writing f(x) = a(x − h)² + k shows the range: (x − h)² takes every value ≥ 0, so f takes every value from k upwards when a > 0, and from k downwards when a < 0.

chapter.title: Is a quadratic on a restricted domain one-one, onto, both or neither?
text: One-one: f(x₁) = f(x₂) only when x₁ = x₂. Onto: every element of the codomain is f(x) for some x in the domain. For a quadratic both depend on where the domain starts compared with the vertex.

Complete the square to find the vertex (h, c). If the domain [d, ∞) starts at or to the right of h, f only increases (one-one) and its range is [f(d), ∞); otherwise f(d) = f(2h − d) and the range is [c, ∞). Compare the range with the codomain.

Complete the square: f(x) = (x − 3)² + 6, so the vertex is at x = 3
One-one (the domain starts at 3, not left of the vertex): yes
Onto (the range is [6, ∞); is every element of the codomain reached?): yes

text: A double inequality is two inequalities at once; do the same thing to all three parts. Dividing by a negative number reverses both signs, so the left and right ends swap places.

chapter.title: Classifying a function as one-one, onto or bijective

text: For ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−ax) dx, integrate by parts once: it becomes (n/a) × ∫₀^∞ xⁿ⁻¹e^(−ax) dx.
Repeat down to ∫₀^∞ e^(−ax) dx = 1/a.
math: Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of e^(−4x) sin x dx.
Use integration by parts twice (or the standard result)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Evaluate ∫ from 0 to ∞ of x⁵ e^(−3x) dx.” A common wrong answer is 40/81.
The power of 3 was taken as 5; the gamma integral gives n!/aⁿ⁺¹, so it is 3⁶.

An integral to ∞ means the limit of the integral to b as b → ∞; when the integrand dies away fast enough, that limit is a finite number. The gamma integral Γ(n + 1) = ∫₀^∞ xⁿe^(−x) dx = n! packages repeated integration by parts.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Integrate by substitution and parts; Evaluate elementary limits. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Find the antiderivative (or use Γ(n + 1)/aⁿ⁺¹ for ∫ xⁿe^(−ax)), evaluate from the lower end to b, and let b → ∞.

modules.title: Centre and radius of a circle from its general equation

chapter.title: Centre and radius of a circle from its general equation
text: Completing the square turns x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 into (x + g)² + (y + f)² = g² + f² − c: a circle with centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).
math: Find the centre and the radius of the circle x² + y² − 10x + 10y + 45 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.
Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: g = −5, f = 5, so the centre is (−g, −f) = (5, −5)
chapter.tip: The centre was read with the wrong signs: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f).

chapter.title: The focus of a parabola
text: y² = 4ax is the set of points as far from the focus (a, 0) as from the directrix x = −a; shifting the vertex to (h, k) shifts the focus by the same amount.
Read the vertex (h, k); set the coefficient of the linear bracket equal to 4a; move a from the vertex along the axis (the direction of the unsquared variable, the sign of a giving the way).
math: Find the coordinates of the focus of the parabola x² = −16y.
Move a units from the vertex along the axis: the focus is (0, −4)

chapter.title: Eccentricity of an ellipse or a hyperbola
text: Eccentricity e = c/a compares the distance from the centre to a focus with the semi-axis on which the foci lie; for an ellipse c² = a² − b² (e < 1), for a hyperbola c² = a² + b² (e > 1).
Write the equation in standard form, decide which axis is the major (or transverse) one, find c² by the right rule, and divide c by that semi-axis.
math: Find the eccentricity of the hyperbola x²/36 − y²/9 = 1.

chapter.title: Areas bounded by a parabola or an ellipse
text: An area between curves is ∫ (top − bottom) dx between the points where they meet; symmetry lets you find one part and multiply.
Sketch the region, find where the curves meet, write the vertical gap (top minus bottom), integrate between the meeting points, and use symmetry (×2 for a parabola about its axis, ×4 for an ellipse).
math: Find the area of the part of the ellipse region that lies in the first quadrant, for the ellipse x²/25 + y² = 1.
Area = ∫ from 0 to 5 of √(1 − x²/25) dx

chapter.title: Which conic does an equation represent?
text: For A x² + C y² + D x + E y + F = 0 (no xy term), the squared terms decide the shape: one squared variable gives a parabola, equal coefficients a circle, same signs an ellipse, opposite signs a hyperbola.
Look only at the x² and y² coefficients first; then, if you want to be sure, complete the squares to see the standard form.
math: Which curve does the equation x² + y² − 4x + 2y − 11 = 0 represent?
Look at the x² and y² coefficients (1 and 1): equal coefficients
So the curve is a circle

screens.title: The method
text: Make the x² and y² coefficients 1 by dividing; halve the x and y coefficients to get g and f; the centre is (−g, −f); r = √(g² + f² − c).
math: Find the centre and the radius of the circle 3x² + 3y² − 18x − 6y − 42 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.
Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: g = −3, f = −1, so the centre is (−g, −f) = (3, 1)

screens.title: Complete the square directly
text: Group the x terms and the y terms: (x² − 4x) + (y² + 6y) = −c.
Add the squares of half the coefficients to both sides: (x − 2)² + (y + 3)² = 4 + 9 − c.
math: Find the centre and the radius of the circle 2x² + 2y² − 12x + 8y + 24 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.
Compare with x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0: g = −3, f = 2, so the centre is (−g, −f) = (3, −2)

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the centre and the radius of the circle 3x² + 3y² − 30x − 18y + 75 = 0. Write them as (h, k, r), where (h, k) is the centre and r is the radius.” A common wrong answer is (−5, −3, 3).
The centre was read with the wrong signs: x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f).
Completing the square turns x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 into (x + g)² + (y + f)² = g² + f² − c: a circle with centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c).

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Simplify radicals. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Make the x² and y² coefficients 1 by dividing; halve the x and y coefficients to get g and f; the centre is (−g, −f); r = √(g² + f² − c).

modules.title: The locus of a point whose distances from two points are in a fixed ratio

chapter.title: The locus of a point whose distances from two points are in a fixed ratio
text: A locus is the set of all points that obey a condition. Writing each distance with the distance formula turns the condition into an equation in x and y.
math: A point P moves so that its distance from A(2, 3) is always 2 times its distance from B(3, 1). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.
Write PA and PB with the distance formula and square PA = 2·PB to remove the roots: (x − 2)² + (y − 3)² = 4[(x − 3)² + (y − 1)²]
Expand the brackets and collect every term on one side: 3x² + 3y² − 20x − 2y + 27 = 0
Divide by 3 so that x² has coefficient 1: x² + y² − (20/3)x − (2/3)y + 9 = 0
chapter.tip: The ratio was applied the other way round (PB = 2·PA). Here P is 2 times as far from A as from B.

chapter.title: The locus of a point equidistant from a point and a line
text: Every point of the locus is as far from the point as from the line, so the two distances can be set equal. The curve is a parabola with S as its focus and the line as its directrix.
For P(x, y), the distance to S comes from the distance formula and the distance to the line x = h is |x − h|. Square both, set them equal, expand, and make x the subject.
math: A point P moves so that it is always the same distance from the point S(−3, 0) as from the line x = 3. Find the equation of the locus of P in the form x = (an expression in y), and type the expression in y.
Expand; the x² terms cancel: −12x = y²

screens.title: The method
text: Let P be (x, y). Write PA and PB with the distance formula, square both sides to remove the roots, expand, collect all terms on one side and divide by the coefficient of x².
math: A point P moves so that its distance from A(−4, −5) is always 2 times its distance from B(−3, −2). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.
Write PA and PB with the distance formula and square PA = 2·PB to remove the roots: (x + 4)² + (y + 5)² = 4[(x + 3)² + (y + 2)²]
Expand the brackets and collect every term on one side: 3x² + 3y² + 16x + 6y + 11 = 0
Divide by 3 so that x² has coefficient 1: x² + y² + (16/3)x + 2y + 11/3 = 0

strategies.title: Check with a point you know is on the locus

screens.title: Check with a point you know is on the locus
text: The point that divides AB internally in the ratio k : 1 is k times as far from A as from B, so it lies on the locus.
Substitute it into your equation: the left-hand side must be 0. If it is not, look for a squaring or sign slip.
math: A point P moves so that its distance from A(−4, 1) is always 3 times its distance from B(−2, −3). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.
Write PA and PB with the distance formula and square PA = 3·PB to remove the roots: (x + 4)² + (y − 1)² = 9[(x + 2)² + (y + 3)²]
Expand the brackets and collect every term on one side: 8x² + 8y² + 28x + 56y + 100 = 0
Divide by 8 so that x² has coefficient 1: x² + y² + (7/2)x + 7y + 25/2 = 0

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “A point P moves so that its distance from A(−3, −4) is always 3 times its distance from B(2, −2). Find the equation of the locus of P. Write it as x² + y² + px + qy + r = 0 (the coefficient of x² must be 1) and type the left-hand side.” A common wrong answer is x² + y² + (29/4)x + (17/2)y + 217/8.
The ratio was applied the other way round (PB = 3·PA). Here P is 3 times as far from A as from B.
A locus is the set of all points that obey a condition. Writing each distance with the distance formula turns the condition into an equation in x and y.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use coordinate distance and section formulas. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Let P be (x, y). Write PA and PB with the distance formula, square both sides to remove the roots, expand, collect all terms on one side and divide by the coefficient of x².

modules.title: The slopes of a pair of lines through the origin

chapter.title: The slopes of a pair of lines through the origin
text: A homogeneous equation ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 factorises into two linear factors through the origin; putting y = mx turns it into a quadratic whose roots are the slopes.
math: The equation 30x² + 11xy + y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Find the slopes of the two lines. Type both, separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Put y = mx and divide by x²: m² + 11m + 30 = 0
Solve the quadratic in m (sum of the roots −11, product 30): the slopes are −6 and −5

chapter.title: The angle between a pair of lines through the origin
text: For ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0 the slopes satisfy m₁ + m₂ = −2h/b and m₁m₂ = a/b, so tan θ = |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)| becomes |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|.
Read a, h (half the xy coefficient) and b, work out h² − ab, and use tan θ = |2√(h² − ab)/(a + b)|.
math: Find tan θ, where θ is the acute angle between the pair of lines 3x² − 4xy + y² = 0.
Compare with ax² + 2hxy + by² = 0: a = 3, h = −2, b = 1

screens.title: The method
text: Substitute y = mx, divide by x², and solve bm² + 2hm + a = 0. Check: the sum of the slopes is −2h/b and the product is a/b.
math: The equation −20x² + 11xy + 3y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Find the slopes of the two lines. Type both, separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Put y = mx and divide by x²: 3m² + 11m − 20 = 0
Solve the quadratic in m (sum of the roots −11/3, product −20/3): the slopes are −5 and 4/3

screens.title: Factorise directly
text: Treat the equation as a quadratic in y and factorise it into (q₁y − p₁x)(q₂y − p₂x).
Each factor set to zero is one line; read off its slope p/q.
math: The equation −5xy + 2y² = 0 represents a pair of straight lines through the origin. Find the slopes of the two lines. Type both, separated by a comma (fractions are fine).
Put y = mx and divide by x²: 2m² − 5m = 0
Solve the quadratic in m (sum of the roots 5/2, product 0): the slopes are 0 and 5/2

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Solve quadratic equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Substitute y = mx, divide by x², and solve bm² + 2hm + a = 0. Check: the sum of the slopes is −2h/b and the product is a/b.

modules.title: The equation of a line through two points

chapter.title: The equation of a line through two points
text: A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so the slope from the two given points fixes its direction, and either point fixes its position.
math: Find the equation of the straight line through A(−1, −5) and B(4, 5). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).
Put A into y = mx + c: c = y₁ − m·x₁ = −3
chapter.tip: The slope was found as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is rise over run, (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

chapter.title: The perpendicular distance from a point to a line
text: The shortest way from a point to a line is along the perpendicular. Its length is |ax₀ + by₀ + c| divided by √(a² + b²), the length of the normal vector (a, b).
Substitute the point into ax + by + c, take the absolute value, and divide by √(a² + b²). Simplify the surd.
math: Find the perpendicular distance from the point (0, 0) to the line 3x + 5y + 4 = 0.
Put the point into ax + by + c: 4

chapter.title: The distance between two parallel lines
text: Parallel lines can be written with the same x and y coefficients; then they differ only in the constant, and the gap between them is |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).
Divide one equation so the x and y coefficients match the other, then use |c₁ − c₂|/√(a² + b²).
math: Find the distance between the parallel lines y + 5 = 0 and y + 11 = 0.
The x and y coefficients already match: y + 11 = 0

chapter.title: The angle between two lines in general form
text: The angle between two lines is the difference of their inclinations, so tan θ = (m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂) from the subtraction formula for tan; the absolute value gives the acute angle.
Find each slope as −a/b, then work out |(m₁ − m₂)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
math: Find tan θ, where θ is the acute angle between the lines 5x + 4y − 4 = 0 and −x + y + 4 = 0.
The slope of ax + by + c = 0 is −a/b: the slopes are −5/4 and 1

chapter.title: Parallel, perpendicular or neither
text: The slope of ax + by + c = 0 is −a/b. Parallel lines have equal slopes; perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is −1.
Find both slopes (or test a₁b₂ − a₂b₁ = 0 for parallel and a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ = 0 for perpendicular, which also works for vertical lines).
math: Are the lines 6x − y + 3 = 0 and 6x − y − 3 = 0 parallel, perpendicular, or neither?

screens.title: The method
text: Find m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁), then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) and rearrange to y = mx + c.
math: Find the equation of the straight line through A(1, 5) and B(3, 4). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).
Put A into y = mx + c: c = y₁ − m·x₁ = 11/2

screens.title: Two-point form
text: Write (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
Cross-multiply and make y the subject.
math: Find the equation of the straight line through A(−1, −2) and B(2, 6). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).
Put A into y = mx + c: c = y₁ − m·x₁ = 2/3

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the equation of the straight line through A(−2, 5) and B(−1, −5). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side (for example 2x − 3).” A common wrong answer is −(1/10)x + 24/5.
The slope was found as (change in x)/(change in y); slope is rise over run, (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).
A straight line has the same slope everywhere, so the slope from the two given points fixes its direction, and either point fixes its position.

modules.title: The tangent or normal to a circle or parabola at a point

chapter.title: The tangent or normal to a circle or parabola at a point
text: The tangent at a point has the slope of the curve there (from implicit differentiation or the standard formulas); the normal is perpendicular to it.
math: Find the equation of the normal to the circle x² + y² = 10 at the point (3, −1). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The slope of the curve x² + y² = 10 at the point (the tangent's slope) is 3
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its slope is −1/3
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y = −(1/3)x
chapter.tip: The tangent was given; the normal is perpendicular to the tangent at the point, so its slope is −1/(tangent slope).

chapter.title: The condition for y = mx + c to be a tangent
text: A line is a tangent when it meets the conic in exactly one point: substituting y = mx + c gives a quadratic in x whose discriminant is 0.
Use the standard conditions: parabola y² = 4ax: c = a/m; circle x² + y² = r²: c² = r²(1 + m²); ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² + b²; hyperbola x²/a² − y²/b² = 1: c² = a²m² − b².
math: Find the positive value of c for which the line y = x + c is a tangent to the ellipse x² + y²/16 = 1.
For this conic, y = mx + c is a tangent when c² = a²m² + b²

screens.title: The method
text: Circle x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁): tangent xx₁ + yy₁ = r². Parabola y² = 4ax at (at², 2at): tangent ty = x + at², normal y = −tx + 2at + at³. Rearrange to y = mx + c.
math: Find the equation of the tangent to the parabola y² = 8x at the point (18, −12). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The slope of the curve y² = 8x at the point (the tangent's slope) is −1/3
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y = −(1/3)x − 6

screens.title: Differentiate implicitly
text: Differentiate the curve's equation with respect to x and solve for dy/dx at the point.
That is the tangent slope; the normal slope is −1 divided by it. Then use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁).
math: Find the equation of the normal to the parabola y² = 20x at the point (5, 10). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.
The slope of the curve y² = 20x at the point (the tangent's slope) is 1
The normal is perpendicular to the tangent: its slope is −1
Use y − y₁ = m(x − x₁): y = −x + 15

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the equation of the tangent to the parabola y² = 16x at the point (36, −24). Write it as y = mx + c and type the right-hand side.” A common wrong answer is 3x − 132.
The normal (the line along the radius or perpendicular to the curve) was given; the tangent touches the curve, perpendicular to the normal.
The tangent at a point has the slope of the curve there (from implicit differentiation or the standard formulas); the normal is perpendicular to it.

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Use straight-line equations. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Circle x² + y² = r² at (x₁, y₁): tangent xx₁ + yy₁ = r². Parabola y² = 4ax at (at², 2at): tangent ty = x + at², normal y = −tx + 2at + at³. Rearrange to y = mx + c.

modules.title: The distance between two points in space

chapter.title: The distance between two points in space
text: In space, Pythagoras is used twice: across the floor (x and y) and then up (z), giving √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).
math: Find the distance between the points P(4, −2, 0) and Q(1, −5, −3).
chapter.tip: The differences were added; in space the straight distance is √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).

chapter.title: The point dividing a segment in space in a ratio
text: The point that divides AB in the ratio m : n is m/(m + n) of the way from A to B, the same in every coordinate.
P = ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n), (mz₂ + nz₁)/(m + n)). For the midpoint, m = n = 1.
math: Find the coordinates of the point that divides the segment from A(0, 0, 5) to B(−1, −1, 3) internally in the ratio 1 : 1 (the midpoint). Type it as (x, y, z).
Weight B by 1 and A by 1: (1·B + 1·A)

chapter.title: Where a point lies in space: octant, plane or axis
text: The three coordinate planes (xy, yz, zx) divide space into eight octants. A zero coordinate puts a point on a coordinate plane; two zeros put it on an axis.

Count the zero coordinates. None: use the signs of x, y and z to name the octant. One zero (say z = 0): the point is in the plane of the other two axes (the xy-plane). Two zeros: the point is on the remaining axis.
math: So the point lies in the yz-plane

screens.title: The method
text: Subtract the coordinates, square each difference, add, and take the square root. Simplify the surd.
math: Find the distance between the points P(−3, 3, 5) and Q(−1, 1, −2).

screens.title: The diagonal of a box
text: Think of a cuboid with edges |Δx|, |Δy| and |Δz|.
The distance between the points is the space diagonal of that box.
math: Find the distance between the points P(4, 3, 2) and Q(2, 2, 0).

screens.title: A common wrong answer
text: A question: “Find the distance between the points P(1, 4, −3) and Q(−1, −4, 4).” A common wrong answer is 17.
The differences were added; in space the straight distance is √(Δx² + Δy² + Δz²).

screens.title: What it uses
text: Each step builds on another skill: Simplify radicals. If a step is slow, practise that skill first.
Then the method is: Subtract the coordinates, square each difference, add, and take the square root. Simplify the surd.

modules.title: Direction cosines of the line through two points

chapter.title: Direction cosines of the line through two points
text: Direction cosines are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the axes; they are the components of a unit vector along the line, so l² + m² + n² = 1.
math: Find the direction cosines of the line through A(−3, 1, −2) and B(4, −1, −2), directed from A to B. Type them as (l, m, n).
Divide each ratio by the length: (7√53/53, −2√53/53, 0)
chapter.tip: These are direction ratios; direction cosines are the ratios divided by the length √53, so that l² + m² + n² = 1.

chapter.title: Parallel, intersecting or skew lines
text: In space two lines are parallel (directions are multiples), intersecting (they share a point), or skew (neither: not parallel and never meet).

If the directions are multiples, the lines are parallel. Otherwise set the general points equal, solve two of the coordinate equations for λ and μ, and test the third: it holds for intersecting lines and fails for skew lines.
math: Are the lines r⃗ = (−î + 2ĵ − 2k̂) + λ(î + ĵ + k̂) and r⃗ = (î + 3ĵ + k̂) + μ(−2î − 2ĵ − 2k̂) parallel, intersecting, or skew?
u × v = (0, 0, 0) (zero means the directions are parallel)
(B − A)·(u × v) = 0 (zero means the lines lie in one plane and meet)

chapter.title: The angle between two lines in space
text: The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors; the dot product gives its cosine, and |u·v| gives the acute angle. cos θ = 0 means the lines are perpendicular.
Take the direction vectors u and v (the vectors multiplied by λ and μ), and work out cos θ = |u·v|/(|u||v|).
math: Find cos θ, where θ is the acute angle between the lines r⃗ = (−2î + ĵ − 2k̂) + λ(−2ĵ + k̂) and r⃗ = (2ĵ) + μ(î + 3ĵ + 2k̂).
Dot product of the direction vectors: u·v = −4

chapter.title: The foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line in space
text: The shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular to the line, so the foot Q is the point of the line with PQ·d = 0.
Write a general point Q = a + λd of the line, form PQ = Q − P, solve PQ·d = 0 for λ, and substitute back.
math: Find the foot of the perpendicular from the point P(4, 2, −2) to the line r⃗ = (2ĵ − 2k̂) + λ(î − k̂). Type it as (x, y, z).
A general point of the line: Q = (0 + λ, 2 + 0λ, −2 + −λ)
PQ is perpendicular to the direction d: (Q − P)·d = 0 gives 2λ = 4, so λ = 2
Put λ = 2 into the general point: (2, 2, −4)

screens.title: The method
text: Find the direction ratios B − A, find the length √(a² + b² + c²), and divide each ratio by it.
math: Find the direction cosines of the line through A(4, −4, 1) and B(0, −1, 4), directed from A to B. Type them as (l, m, n).

chapter.title: A statement and its converse
text: The converse of 'if P then Q' is 'if Q then P'. A statement can be true while its converse is false, so each needs its own check.

At n = 6 the value is 203 = 7 × 29, not prime

modules.title: Principal values of inverse trigonometric functions

chapter.title: Principal values of inverse trigonometric functions
text: Each inverse function returns one angle from its principal range: sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹ in [−π/2, π/2]; cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹ in [0, π]. That is why it has a single value.

chapter.title: sin⁻¹(sin θ), cos⁻¹(cos θ) and tan⁻¹(tan θ)
text: sin⁻¹(sin θ) is the angle in [−π/2, π/2] with the same sine as θ; it equals θ only when θ is already in that range (similarly [0, π] for cos⁻¹ and (−π/2, π/2) for tan⁻¹).
Find an angle in the principal range with the same ratio: use sin(π − θ) = sin θ, cos(2π − θ) = cos θ, tan(θ − π) = tan θ, and add or remove whole turns.

2π/3 has the same ratio as −π/3 (a whole number of turns removed)

cot⁻¹ x = tan⁻¹(1/x) for x > 0, and π + tan⁻¹(1/x) for x < 0.
